lessonTitle: Inside a plant: sensors, PLCs, RTUs, HMIs, historians and SIS
question: A refinery's safety system is designed so that it can still shut the unit down even if the main control system has crashed. Which design property is this?
options: Redundancy of the historian
Independence of the SIS from the BPCS
Real-time scheduling of the HMI
Remote access to field sites
explain: NIST describes the SIS as often independent from other control systems so that a BPCS failure does not harm SIS function. That independence is exactly what attackers in the Triton case worked to get around.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Modbus/TCP byte by byte, and why it trusts everyone
question: A server replies with function code 0x83 and one data byte 0x02. What happened?
options: A successful read of 2 registers
A new function code 0x83 the server supports
A write of value 2
An exception to a Read Holding Registers (03) request, with exception code 2
explain: Exception replies set the high bit: 0x80 + 0x03 = 0x83. Exception code 02 is 'illegal data address' in the spec. A burst of exceptions often means someone is probing addresses.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Ukraine 2015 and Industroyer 2016
question: Why did ESET judge Industroyer more dangerous than the 2015 toolset?
options: It encrypted files for ransom
It was signed with stolen certificates
It spread by USB
It implemented four industrial protocols itself, so it could command switches and breakers directly without the operators' software
explain: ESET: the authors 'went to great lengths to create malware capable of directly controlling switches and circuit breakers', speaking IEC 101, IEC 104, IEC 61850 and OPC DA. A tool like that can be reused at other utilities with the same protocols.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Watching OT: asset inventory and passive monitoring
question: The Suricata Modbus rules never fire, even in a test with real write traffic. What is the most likely cause?
options: Modbus writes cannot be detected
Suricata needs encryption keys
The sid numbers are too high
The Modbus app-layer parser is disabled by default in suricata.yaml, so 'alert modbus' rules have nothing to match
explain: Suricata ships with the Modbus parser disabled. Enable it and set detection port 502; its docs also advise unlimited stream reassembly depth for long-lived Modbus connections.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Inside a SAML response: Issuer, Subject, Conditions and statements
question: An assertion for `https://payroll.example.com` is presented, within its time window and with a valid signature, to `https://wiki.example.com`. What should the wiki do?
options: Accept it, since the IdP signed it
Accept it but log a warning
Reject it: its AudienceRestriction does not name the wiki
Forward it to the payroll app
explain: The Audience says which SP the IdP meant the statement for. A genuine signature only proves who issued it. Accepting another SP's assertion would let any app that receives assertions log in as its users elsewhere.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Case: ruby-saml CVE-2024-45409 and the GitLab SAML bypass (2024)
question: Why did enabling MFA at the IdP not protect GitLab instances from CVE-2024-45409?
options: The IdP's MFA was too weak
GitLab ignores IdP MFA by design
The forged response was presented directly to GitLab; the IdP was never asked to authenticate anyone
The flaw was in the IdP
explain: An SP-side verification bypass means the attacker constructs the response and posts it to the SP. Controls that live at the IdP never run. GitLab's mitigation was a second factor at GitLab itself.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: SCIM provisioning: creating and removing accounts in every app
question: A company uses JIT provisioning only. Ana leaves and is disabled at the IdP. What remains in each app?
options: Nothing: JIT accounts are deleted at logout
Only Ana's email address
Ana's app account, with whatever data and API keys it holds, because the app is never told Ana left
A SCIM error
explain: JIT creates accounts on login and hears nothing on departure. The account and anything attached to it stay until someone removes them, which is why push provisioning or regular access reviews are needed.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Case: Okta's support system and the stolen HAR files (2023)
question: Which control would have made the stolen HAR session tokens fail when replayed from the attacker's network?
options: A stronger password policy
Longer session lifetimes
Binding admin sessions to the network (ASN) they were created on, so reuse from elsewhere forces reauthentication
Encrypting HAR files at rest in the support system
explain: The tokens were valid sessions; passwords were never involved. Okta's remediation was exactly session binding for admins. Encrypting files at rest would not help against an actor using a legitimate service account that can read them.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Leavers: deprovisioning, SCIM and the Cash App download
question: Block's filing says the former employee had regular access to the reports in a past role, and used it after leaving. Which control most directly addresses that failure?
options: Stronger password rules for employees
Removing every entitlement, including in tools with local accounts, at termination, then reconciling to catch misses
Encrypting the reports at rest
Requiring employees to sign a non-disclosure agreement
explain: The access itself outlived the job. Complete deprovisioning, including applications outside single sign-on, and reconciliation to catch what was missed, address that directly. Encryption at rest does not stop an authorised account from reading data.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Privileged access: why admin rights differ, and the Snowden case
question: Ana is a domain administrator who also reads email and browses the web all day on the same account. Which NIST control does this break, and why does it matter?
options: AC-6(2): privileged users should use a non-privileged account for non-security work, so a phishing email does not land on an admin account
PS-4: Ana has not left the company
AC-2(3): Ana's account is not dormant
IA-5(7): there is no embedded password
explain: AC-6(2) separates everyday work from admin work. If the account that opens attachments is also a domain admin, any malware it runs starts with domain admin rights.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Just-in-time admin and break-glass accounts
question: A tenant makes every Global Administrator and Privileged Role Administrator assignment eligible, requires approval to activate, and the only approvers have left the company. What happens, and what prevents it?
options: Activation is approved automatically after 24 hours
Nobody can activate, so administration is locked; tested break-glass accounts with permanently active rights prevent it
HR can approve activations instead
The eligible users become active automatically
explain: Microsoft documents this exact lockout. Its emergency access guidance makes break-glass accounts permanently active Global Administrators, outside the approval flow, protected by phishing-resistant credentials and alerting.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Solving for a homography with the DLT, by hand
question: You pick four matches for the DLT, but three of them lie on one straight line. What happens?
options: The DLT still works because 8 equations are enough
SVD returns the identity matrix
The fourth point is automatically ignored
The solution is degenerate: A loses rank and H is not determined
explain: Collinear points do not pin down the projective map; the system has a bigger null space and many H fit. OpenCV's findHomography docs say its robust methods discard collinear 4-point subsets for this reason.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Events, alerts and incidents: when does it become an incident?
question: Antivirus in monitor mode logs that Mimikatz ran on a finance PC. Nothing else is known yet. What is the best classification?
options: An incident: unauthorised code ran, so integrity is already jeopardized
A routine event, because the tool did not block anything
An adverse event to keep watching, with no declaration until data is lost
A false positive until a second tool confirms it
explain: The NIST definition covers occurrences that actually or imminently jeopardize integrity or confidentiality. Credential-dumping code running on a host already does. Waiting for data loss is how the HSE detection on 31 March became a nationwide outage on 14 May.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Containment: isolate, watch, disable, block, and the trade-offs
question: Which is the strongest reason NIST gives against prolonged "watch the attacker" containment?
options: The attacker can escalate access or compromise other systems while you watch, and the organisation may be liable
It is illegal everywhere
It produces too much log data
Attackers always notice monitoring
explain: NIST calls delayed containment dangerous because the attacker could escalate unauthorised access or compromise other systems, and recommends discussing any sandbox strategy with legal first.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Windows artefacts: event logs, Prefetch, Amcache, Shimcache, MFT
question: A suspicious EXE appears in Shimcache, and nowhere else: no Prefetch file, no 4688 event, no EDR record. What can you conclude?
options: It definitely ran
Shimcache is unreliable, so ignore it
It existed on the host at some point, but execution is not proven
The attacker must have deleted the Prefetch file
explain: Shimcache can record files that were present but not executed. Treat it as evidence of presence and look for other execution artefacts before concluding it ran.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Eradication and recovery: rebuild, credentials, krbtgt and backups
question: Why does Microsoft say to reset the krbtgt password twice, with at least 10 hours in between?
options: The account keeps the two most recent passwords; the second reset removes the stolen one from the history, and the wait lets legitimate tickets expire normally
The first reset often fails silently
Domain controllers replicate only on the second change
Ten hours is how long a reset takes to replicate
explain: With a history of two, the stolen key is still in the history after one reset; the second reset pushes it out. The wait matches the default maximum ticket lifetime (10 hours), so tickets issued before the first reset have expired first.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Blameless postmortems, lessons learned and tabletop exercises
question: A postmortem says: "Root cause: the on-call analyst ignored the alert." Why would a blameless review reject this as the conclusion?
options: Because it names a person and stops there; the review should ask why the alert was easy to miss (volume, routing, ownership, monitor mode) and fix that
Because analysts never make mistakes
Because alerts are not part of IR
Because only executives can be named
explain: Blameless reviews look for systemic causes. If one tired person could miss it, the next one can too; the fix is in the system (alert design, ownership, staffing), which NIST r3 calls the underlying or systemic root cause.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Beyond the login: UNION, blind and second-order injection
question: A search page shows no results and catches every database error, but it responds about five seconds slower for some inputs. What does this suggest?
options: Nothing: without visible output, SQL injection cannot be exploited
A UNION attack, since UNION queries are always slower
A cross-site scripting bug
Possible time-based blind injection: response time can leak whether an injected condition is true
explain: Blind injection needs only an observable difference. Time is observable. If an injected condition can make the query pause, the attacker learns one bit per request, and tools can repeat that thousands of times.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: ORMs, stored procedures and least-privilege accounts
question: A Java app calls a stored procedure with `prepareCall("{call find_user(?)}")` and `setString(1, input)`. Inside, the procedure builds a query with `'... WHERE name = ''' + @name + ''''` and runs it with EXEC. Is the app safe from SQL injection?
options: Yes, because the call uses a placeholder
Yes, because stored procedures cannot be injected
No: the input arrives safely as a value, but the procedure pastes it into new SQL text and runs it
No, because CallableStatement does not support parameters
explain: Binding protects the call, not the dynamic SQL constructed inside the procedure. The fix is inside the procedure: bind the value in the dynamic query (sp_executesql with parameters in SQL Server, EXECUTE ... USING in PostgreSQL) or avoid dynamic SQL.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Shellshock: when an environment variable became code
question: A Python CGI script, not a bash script, runs `os.system("/usr/bin/uptime")` with no user input in the command. Was it exposed to Shellshock on a server with vulnerable bash as /bin/sh?
options: No: the command contains no user input
Yes: os.system starts a shell, which inherits the HTTP_ variables from CGI and parses them at startup
No: Python scripts are immune
Only if the script was run as root
explain: The attacker's data is in the environment, not the command line. os.system runs /bin/sh -c, and a vulnerable bash as /bin/sh imports function-like variables at startup and runs the trailing code.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: The defence map: validation, encoding, parameters and detection
question: Your PostgreSQL log suddenly shows dozens of `permission denied for table users` errors from the web application's account. What is the most likely explanation and first step?
options: Normal behaviour; ignore it
A disk failure; restore from backup
Something, possibly injected SQL, is asking for data the app was never granted; find the requests behind it in the access logs and treat it as a likely attack
The password column is corrupted
explain: A correct application never queries tables it lacks rights to, so these errors usually mean a bug or injection probing. Least privilege stopped the read; correlate timestamps with web logs to find the endpoint and input.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
question: A configuration service does about 50 small reads per second in short bursts, on a 2-core VM that is already busy. A teammate proposes `IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL` to save system calls. Good idea?
options: Yes, SQPOLL always lowers latency
Yes, but only with IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL as well
No: at 50 I/O per second the syscalls saved are negligible, and the poll thread competes for one of only 2 busy CPUs and keeps going to sleep between bursts
No, because SQPOLL requires root on all kernels
explain: SQPOLL pays off when a stream of submissions keeps the thread busy. Here it would mostly spin or sleep and wake, costing CPU on a constrained machine for almost no saved work. Privilege is no longer required on recent kernels, so that is not the reason.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Gadgets: from a polluted prototype to code execution (Kibana)
question: After upgrading to a Node.js release that includes pull requests 48726 and 53781, a team decides their unpatched deep-merge helper is no longer a risk. Why is that wrong?
options: The pull requests hardened only Node.js's own child_process option handling; other gadgets in frameworks, libraries and the app still read polluted properties
Those changes only apply when Node.js runs with --permission
The changes were reverted because the Node.js threat model rejects them
Prototype pollution only matters in browsers, so the helper was never a risk
explain: The hardening stops child_process from reading env, shell and similar options from the prototype. Logic gadgets (isAdmin), request options, template engine options and countless library defaults are untouched. The source still has to be fixed.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: eval, new Function and why node:vm is not a sandbox
question: A SaaS (software as a service) product lets customers upload JavaScript 'rules' and runs them with `vm.runInNewContext(rule, { order })`. What is the core problem?
options: runInNewContext is slower than eval
Customers cannot use modern syntax in a vm context
node:vm is documented as not a security mechanism; shared objects such as order lead back to the host's Function constructor and from there to process
The rule cannot read order because contexts share nothing
explain: The Node.js docs say not to use node:vm for untrusted code. Anything passed in, like order, carries a constructor chain back to the host realm. Use a separate, low-privilege process or a non-code rules format.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Middleware and internal headers: the Next.js bypass
question: Why did the fix for CVE-2025-29927 generate a random ID at server start instead of simply removing the recursion check?
options: Because random IDs make the server faster
Because the header was required by HTTP/2
Because the recursion guard is still needed for the server's own subrequests; the ID lets the server prove a marker came from itself, and markers without it are dropped
Because the ID encrypts the response
explain: The guard prevents middleware from looping on the server's own inner fetches, so it has to stay. What was missing was authentication of the signal. A per-process secret known only to the server separates its own markers from forged ones.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Finding and catching JavaScript bugs: tools, signals, practice
question: After a confirmed prototype pollution incident on a Node.js API, the team deploys the fixed merge function. Which step must not be skipped?
options: Clearing the browser cache of every user
Restarting every process that ran the vulnerable code, because the polluted Object.prototype persists in memory until the process exits
Rotating the TLS certificate
Reinstalling Node.js
explain: Fixing the code stops new pollution but does not undo pollution already in a running process's heap. If a gadget reached code execution, rebuild hosts and rotate secrets as well.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
question: A latency-sensitive service shows p99 spikes every few seconds, and a profile shows time in page faults right after memory was purged. Which change targets this most directly?
options: Increase the number of size classes
Disable the thread cache
Lengthen the purge delay (jemalloc dirty_decay_ms or MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY) so freed pages stay mapped longer between bursts
Lower jemalloc's opt.narenas to 1
explain: The spikes come from returning pages to the OS and faulting them back in. A longer delay keeps them resident across bursts, at the cost of higher RSS. Disabling caches or arenas adds contention without fixing the faults.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: The nemesis: partitions, pauses, clocks and crashes
question: A coordination service hands out locks that expire if the holder misses heartbeats for 2 s. Which nemesis is most likely to show two clients holding the same lock?
options: Process pauses with SIGSTOP and SIGCONT lasting longer than the lease
A partition that isolates one follower that holds no locks
Bit flips in a log file on a single node
Packet duplication on a client link
explain: A paused holder cannot notice its lease expiring, so another client acquires the lock, and the first resumes believing it still holds it. Isolating an uninvolved follower or flipping bits does not target the lease mechanism.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Prune before you measure: shared memory and registers
question: A config that uses 144 KiB of shared memory tunes fine on a cc 9.0 GPU. The same tuning job runs on a cc 8.6 GPU and that config is now rejected. What should the tuner do?
options: Reduce num_stages automatically until it fits and keep the measured timing
Treat the limit as device state: prune against this device's limit and re-tune, because the legal space itself changed
Keep the cc 9.0 result, since the config is still correct code
Fail the tuning run, because the config list is invalid
explain: Shared memory per block is a documented per-capability quantity (227 KB at 9.0, 99 KB at 8.6), so the set of legal configurations is part of the device, not the kernel. Silently rewriting num_stages produces a config nobody measured, and carrying the old winner over is exactly the stale-cache failure of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Handing the device to user space: vfio-pci, BARs and DMA memory
question: Why do DPDK and SPDK allocate I/O buffers from hugepages rather than plain malloc memory?
options: Because NICs cannot DMA into 4 KiB pages
Because VFIO only accepts 1 GiB pages
Because hugepages are faster for the device to read over PCIe
Because hugepages have physical addresses that Linux does not move today and are contiguous within a page, and they also cut TLB misses
explain: The device must be given addresses that stay valid. Hugepages are not migrated by Linux today and each one is physically contiguous; the TLB benefit is a bonus. With an IOMMU, VFIO pins and maps them explicitly.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
question: A key-value service handles 50,000 requests per second per machine, shares cores with other services, and runs on laptops for development. Should it adopt DPDK?
options: Probably not: per-request kernel overhead is a tiny part of its budget, and bypass would burn dedicated cores, need root-level device setup and lose kernel tooling
Yes, bypass always lowers latency
Yes, but only with UIO to avoid needing an IOMMU
Yes, because hugepages alone will double its throughput
explain: At 50k requests per second each request has about 20 us of one core, so saving a microsecond of kernel path is noise. Bypass pays off near line rate, not for ordinary services.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
question: A fused kernel for a long row-wise reduction starts spilling registers and runs slower than two unfused kernels. Which fix matches what FlashAttention and Triton tutorials do?
options: Tile the reduction so each block of the row fits on chip, carrying running statistics between tiles
Fuse even more ops into the kernel
Switch to FP64 to get more registers
Disable the GPU's L2 cache
explain: Fusion is bounded by on-chip capacity. Tiling with running statistics (as in FlashAttention's online softmax) keeps the working set small while still avoiding HBM round trips for intermediates.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
question: Two runs differ only in schedule: 30 epochs and 9,600 epochs. Following Beyer et al.'s ImageNet table, which setup should win each run?
options: Function matching wins both; mixup always helps
Consistent teaching wins the short run; function matching wins the long run
The fixed teacher wins the short run, because caching is cheaper per step
All three tie at 9,600 epochs because every student eventually matches the teacher
explain: At 30 epochs consistent teaching leads (74.95% vs 73.89% for function matching). At 9,600 epochs function matching is best (82.31%), consistent teaching close behind (81.76%), and the fixed teacher has overfit (76.95%). Mixup only pays off when there is time to fit the harder inputs.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: An LLM distillation pipeline: logits, tokenizers, traces, compute
question: Your teacher uses a 150k-entry tokenizer and your student a 32k one, but you do have the teacher's full logits. Which option gives a logit-level signal at all?
options: Token-level forward KL after truncating the teacher to 32k entries
Token-level reverse KL, which does not need a shared vocabulary
On-policy GKD with beta = 0.5
ULD: sort both distributions at each position, pad, and penalize the absolute differences
explain: Every KL or JSD variant compares probabilities of the same token, which needs a shared vocabulary; truncating to 32k entries does not make the ids mean the same strings. ULD compares sorted probability vectors, so it only transfers the shape of the distribution, but it works across tokenizers. Seq-KD on generated text is the other option.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
question: A colleague quantizes both keys and values per-token at 2 bits and sees accuracy collapse, while 4-bit per-token worked fine. What is the most likely fix?
options: Use 3-bit per-token for both
Quantize values per-channel and keep keys per-token
Quantize keys per-channel and keep values per-token
Add more calibration data
explain: Per-token key groups get their range stretched by outlier channels, which wipes out the small channels at 2 bits. Per-channel keys fix that. In KIVI's Llama-2-13B test, keys per-token with values per-channel scored 2.80 on CoQA, worse than all per-token.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
question: Using the bars, which move gives the larger capacity gain over GQA-8 BF16: FP8, or keeping 20% of tokens in BF16?
options: FP8, about 2x
They are equal
20% kept, about 5x
Neither changes capacity
explain: FP8 halves bytes per token (59 to 119 sequences). Keeping 20% of tokens cuts per-sequence cache 5x (59 to 297), but with the risk of losing information permanently.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
question: A chatbot has 1,000 active sessions that each return every 5 minutes, and the host tier holds 600 sessions. Under strict LRU, what hit rate should you expect for returning sessions, and why?
options: About 60%, because the tier holds 60% of sessions
100%, because LRU keeps recently active sessions
About 50%, because LRU and FIFO behave the same here
Close to 0%, because each session is the least recently used by the time it returns, so it was just evicted
explain: With a cyclic access pattern larger than the cache, LRU evicts the oldest session, which is exactly the next one to return. Every return misses. Admission filtering that keeps a fixed subset resident, a bigger tier (SSD) or scheduler look-ahead all fix this; matching capacity alone does not.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
question: A node is at (10, 3). It performs a local event when its physical clock reads 11. What timestamp does the event get?
explain: l = max(10, 11) = 11, which differs from the old l, so c resets to 0: (11, 0). The reset is what keeps c bounded: as soon as the physical clock catches up with l, all accumulated ties are forgotten.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Inside the encoders: markers, [MASK] padding and training
question: A user types the 3-word query *who founded pixar*. With the default query length of 32, how many query vectors take part in MaxSim?
options: 3, one per word
4, one per WordPiece token
7, the tokens plus [CLS], [Q] and [SEP]
32, because the query is padded with [MASK] to 32 positions and every position yields a vector
explain: ColBERT pads every query to N_q = 32 with [MASK] tokens, and every position's output vector is used in MaxSim. So the query matrix is always 32 x 128, and the mask vectors act as learned expansion terms.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
question: In one step of ordinary CoT decoding, which operation discards the most information about the model's internal state?
options: The attention layers, because they average over earlier positions
Sampling a single token from softmax(W h), since only its identity is passed on
The final layer normalization before the LM head
The positional encoding added to the next input
explain: The next pass sees only e(x) for the one sampled token, a vector chosen from a fixed table of 50,257 rows. Everything else in the 768-dimensional h(t), including how probable the alternatives were, is dropped. Attention and normalization transform information but pass a full vector on.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
question: Adding 6 pause tokens vs. adding 6 Coconut thoughts to a 12-layer model: what happens to the longest serial chain of layer computations before the answer?
options: Both grow to 84 layers
Pause: stays 12. Coconut: grows to about 84
Pause: grows to 84. Coconut: stays 12
Both stay at 12 because attention is parallel
explain: A pause slot's input is a fixed embedding, so its computation happens in the same pass and every path climbs at most 12 layers. Each Coconut thought is the top-layer output of the previous pass fed in at the bottom, so 6 thoughts plus the final pass give 7 x 12 = 84.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: PGM-index: guaranteed error with optimal linear segments
question: Why can uniform random keys need about as many segments as log-normal keys at epsilon 8?
options: The greedy algorithm is not optimal for uniform data
Uniform keys have duplicates
Linear models cannot represent a uniform CDF
At small scale, random gaps make the positions deviate from any line by more than 8 slots, so the distribution's global shape barely matters
explain: The uniform CDF is a straight line globally, but the actual positions of random keys wander around that line, and over 400,000 keys those excursions exceed 8 slots often. With a larger epsilon the wiggles fit inside the band and uniform data collapses to a single segment at eps 512. Model the data you have, not the distribution it came from.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index
question: In doc-only mode, what work remains at query time?
options: Tokenizing the query and traversing the inverted index
Running the full transformer on the query
Re-encoding every candidate document
Nothing; results are precomputed per query
explain: The query is tokenized with the same vocabulary and each token gets a fixed weight (1 in SPLADE-doc, or a lookup table in OpenSearch). No transformer runs at query time.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: RankNet: a probability for every pair
question: Two documents with different labels currently have identical scores. What is the RankNet cost of that pair (sigma = 1)?
options: 0, because the scores are not in the wrong order
ln 2, about 0.693, so the pair is still pushed apart
Infinite, because the probability is undefined
1, the maximum of the sigmoid
explain: At s_i = s_j the sigmoid gives P = 0.5 and C = ln(1 + e^0) = ln 2. Burges calls this a built-in margin: equal scores for differently labeled documents are still penalized.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
question: Why does regrouping $(QK^\top)V$ as $Q(K^\top V)$ fail for softmax attention?
options: Matrix multiplication is not associative
The softmax is applied to each row of $QK^\top$ before multiplying by V, so the product cannot be regrouped
Softmax attention uses different key and query dimensions
The causal mask makes regrouping impossible for any attention
explain: Associativity only holds for plain products. Softmax applies a nonlinear exp and normalization to every entry of $QK^\top$ first. Causal masking alone is fine: the running sum $S_t$ handles it.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Chunkwise DeltaNet derived: WY form and the UT transform by hand
question: In the toy, $k_A^\top k_B=0$, yet $T$ has 0.48 in row 3, column 1. Why?
options: Rounding error in the triangular solve
Because beta = 1 makes T symmetric
Because the diagonal of T is always 1
Token 1 changed $w_2$, and $w_2$ feeds token 3: an indirect path through token 2
explain: T counts every path. Token 1 affects token 2 with weight -0.6 and token 2 affects token 3 with weight -0.8, so the indirect effect is 0.48 even though the direct edge is 0. T is lower triangular, not symmetric.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view
question: On a server you find a process whose /proc/<pid>/exe link reads /tmp/.cache/kworker (deleted). What is the most reasonable reading?
options: Normal: kernel worker threads always run from /tmp
Suspicious: a program was started from a world-writable directory and its file was then removed
Harmless: (deleted) only means the process has exited
Proof that the disk is failing
explain: Kernel threads have no executable file at all, and a process that has exited has no /proc directory. A running program whose file lived in /tmp and was deleted after starting is a common way to leave fewer traces on disk, so it deserves investigation.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: sudo and sudoers: controlled, logged use of root
question: A rule says `bob ALL = (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/less /var/log/syslog`. Why is this close to giving bob full root?
options: Because NOPASSWD rules are ignored
Because /var/log/syslog contains root's password
Because less can start a shell from inside, and that shell would run as root
It is not; bob can only read one file
explain: less, like many pagers and editors, can run a shell command from within. Since less runs as root under sudo, that shell is a root shell. Use a read-only alternative, NOEXEC, or give bob group read access to the log instead.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
question: After setting PasswordAuthentication no, which attack is still fully possible?
options: Online password guessing against sshd
Reading passwords off the network
Logging in to accounts with empty passwords
Logging in with a public key an intruder appended to a user's authorized_keys
explain: Disabling passwords stops guessing and empty-password logins. A key added to authorized_keys still authenticates normally, which is why that file is a favourite persistence spot.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: A basic hardening checklist and where to practise
question: Which control helps against the most cases in this course, and what is its blind spot?
options: Disabling password SSH; it does nothing for local bugs
Removing setuid bits; it breaks passwd
Patching; it cannot help before a fix exists, as with the xz backdoor before discovery
Log shipping; it prevents nothing
explain: Every case was fixed by an update, but updates arrive only after someone finds the bug. That window is why exposure limits, least privilege, logs and baselines are layered on top.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tailoring, exceptions and rolling a baseline out safely
question: An auditor finds that 40 hosts have had a failing SSH rule for a year, each with a waiver that says 'temporary, ops team'. What process fix matters most?
options: Delete the rule from the benchmark
Give every waiver an end date and a named owner, and have the checker treat expired waivers as failures
Stop scanning those 40 hosts
Move the hosts to the Level 2 profile
explain: A waiver without an expiry is a permanent silent exception. Expiry dates checked by the tool force a decision: renew with a reason, fix the host, or tailor the profile for that host class.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Writing audit rules that answer real questions
question: On an x86-64 server your only execve rule is `-F arch=b64 -S execve`. What can an attacker do?
options: Nothing: b64 covers every call on a 64-bit kernel
Disable auditd without root
Run programs through the 32-bit system call interface, which this rule never evaluates
Read your rules file
explain: The 32-bit ABI has its own syscall numbers and audit evaluates it separately. Add the same rule with -F arch=b32 (and consider SystemCallArchitectures=native for services, lesson 5).

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tetragon: filtering and enforcing inside the kernel
question: Why does a sensor hook security_file_permission rather than reading the file name from the openat() system call arguments?
options: openat() cannot be traced
The hook sees the kernel's resolved file, which user space cannot change after the check, avoiding TOCTOU races on syscall arguments
security_file_permission runs in user space
It is faster to write in YAML
explain: Syscall arguments live in user memory and can be changed between when a sensor reads them and when the kernel uses them. The LSM hook runs on the kernel's own file object.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Patching a fleet: automatic updates, restarts, reboots and rings
question: A critical OpenSSL fix was installed on every host last night and the dashboard shows 100% patched. Which hosts are still exposed?
options: None: installed means fixed
Hosts where services linked to the old library were not restarted, since they still run the old code in memory
Only hosts without unattended-upgrades
Hosts with livepatch enabled
explain: A library update takes effect for a process only when it restarts. needrestart exists to find and restart those services. Livepatch is for the kernel, not user-space libraries.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a fleet plan, and where to practise
question: Which statement about this course's tools is accurate?
options: OpenSCAP blocks attacks in real time
Falco enforces policy by killing processes by default
auditd and eBPF sensors make patching unnecessary
Assessment tools (OpenSCAP) find drift from a baseline; telemetry tools (audit, Falco, Tetragon) record or act on what happens; neither replaces patching
explain: Assessment compares configuration with the baseline on a schedule. Telemetry watches activity; Tetragon can also enforce. None of them removes a vulnerability; patching and rebuilding do.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
question: Your pairwise judge compares old ranker versus new ranker results and always shows the new ranker's result first. It reports a 58% win rate for the new ranker. What should you do first?
options: Ship the new ranker, 58% is a clear win
Rerun every comparison with the order swapped and count a win only when both orders agree; inconsistent pairs become ties
Switch to a longer prompt so the judge reads more carefully
Ask the judge to explain its reasoning and trust the explanation
explain: With a fixed order, position bias is confounded with the treatment. Swap-and-tie (Zheng et al.) removes the position effect: wins must survive both orders. Randomising the order per pair is the cheaper large-scale alternative.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
question: Your new prompt makes answers about twice as long, and your LLM judge's pairwise win rate jumps from 50% to 68%. What is the best next step?
options: Ship it: 68% is a clear win
Check whether the gain survives at matched length, for example with a length-controlled regression or a human review of a sample
Switch the judge to single-answer grading, which has no length bias
Shorten the old answers by truncation and re-run
explain: Dubois et al. showed verbosity alone can move a win rate by tens of points. Estimate the preference at equal length (or ask people) before attributing the gain to quality. Single-answer grading is not immune to length bias, and truncation damages the baseline.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Task-specific eval sets, regression tests and significance
question: You want to detect a 2-point change in pass rate, and the per-item difference has standard deviation about 0.4. Roughly how many items do you need for a 95% half-width of 0.02?
options: About 160
About 400
About 1,500
About 10,000
explain: n is about (1.96 x 0.4 / 0.02) squared = 39.2 squared, about 1,537 items. Small eval sets can only detect large changes.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Measuring a guard, and why no guard is complete
question: A guard has recall 0.9 and false positive rate 0.05. Harmful traffic is 0.5% of requests. Roughly what fraction of blocked requests are actually harmful?
options: About 8%
About 50%
About 90%
About 95%
explain: Precision = 0.9 x 0.005 / (0.9 x 0.005 + 0.05 x 0.995) = 0.0045 / 0.05425, about 0.083. With rare harm, even a 5% FPR means most blocks hit benign users.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
question: In the contiguous simulation, 12.8% of the pool was free yet the next request in line could not start. Which kind of waste is this?
options: Internal fragmentation
Reserved slots
Activation memory
External fragmentation
explain: Free memory existed, but not as one contiguous run long enough for the waiting request's reservation. That is external fragmentation. With fixed-size blocks any free block is usable, so external fragmentation disappears; the 0.5% left free in the paged run is just too few blocks for the next prompt.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Few-shot examples and asking the model to reason first
question: Your sentiment prompt has four examples, all labeled positive, and the model now labels most neutral reviews positive. What is the most likely cause?
options: Four examples are too few for in-context learning
The examples are not diverse, so the model picked up 'answer positive' as part of the pattern
Examples only affect format, never labels
The model needs gradient updates to learn labels
explain: Examples teach whatever pattern they share, intended or not. Anthropic's advice is to make examples diverse and to cover edge cases. Brown et al. show that examples steer behavior with no gradient updates at all.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
question: A summarization job uses a strict schema with max_tokens set to 200. About 3 percent of replies fail to parse even though constrained decoding is on. What is the most likely cause?
options: The decoder's mask has a bug that lets invalid tokens through
Those replies hit the 200-token limit and were cut off mid-JSON
The model refused, which always produces invalid JSON
JSON Schema cannot describe summaries
explain: A mask keeps every prefix valid and allows stopping only at an accept state, but the token limit cuts generation off regardless. Check the stop reason (max_tokens or incomplete) and raise the limit or shorten the output.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
question: Which cache key is safest for storing parsed filter objects?
options: The raw query string exactly as typed
The normalized query string alone
The normalized query plus the user's session ID
The normalized query plus the schema version and vocabulary version
explain: Raw strings fragment the cache on case and spacing. Without versions, a schema or dictionary change keeps serving stale parses (an old field name, a city ID that was split). The session ID would make the cache nearly useless, since the parse does not depend on who asked.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
question: At k=100, L=100, w=20, FIRST brings our modeled query latency from 10.35 s to 2.39 s. Which next change cuts FIRST's latency the most?
options: Raising the window step s while keeping w = 20, which removes windows and their prefill
Asking for a shorter permutation format
Using a higher sampling temperature
Adding a reasoning step before the ranking
explain: FIRST has no permutation to shorten, so the remaining time is prefill on a chain of windows. Fewer windows (or fewer tokens per window) is what is left. A reasoning step would add decode tokens back.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
question: Your API returns only generated text, no log-probabilities. Which pointwise method can you still run, and with what limitation?
options: Query likelihood, because it uses teacher forcing
Neither; pointwise prompts cannot work without fine-tuning
Yes/No generation, but you only get a binary label, so many passages tie and the ranking is coarse
Both, as long as you set temperature to 0
explain: Query likelihood needs the probability of the given query tokens, which a text-only API cannot provide. Yes/No still produces an answer, but without p(Yes) you only get two buckets, so passages inside a bucket keep their original order.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
question: Your listwise reranker works well on BM25 input but degrades badly when you switch the first stage to a new retriever that returns candidates in a near-random order. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Increase the window step so fewer windows are needed
Lower the temperature to 0
Shuffle the input several times and aggregate the rankings, or use a student trained with shuffled inputs
Switch to query likelihood, which is order-free but needs no changes
explain: The symptom is order sensitivity: failures and the one-pass guarantee both lean on a good initial order. Permutation self-consistency marginalizes the order out, and RankVicuna/RankZephyr train on shuffled inputs for the same reason. Temperature 0 makes outputs repeatable, not order-invariant.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Evaluating routers: cost-quality curves, PGR, APGR and CPT
question: A router has r = 7.6 on a benchmark where the weak model scores 6.5 and the strong model 8.4. What is its PGR?
explain: PGR = (7.6 - 6.5) / (8.4 - 6.5) = 1.1 / 1.9 = 0.579. 0.905 is 7.6 / 8.4, which ignores the weak baseline; 0.421 is 1 minus the right answer.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
question: You lower the ratio threshold from 0.8 to 0.6. What happens?
options: More matches survive and the outlier fraction rises
Nothing, since the ratio is scale-free
Every correct match is kept and only outliers are removed
Fewer matches survive and the surviving set has a lower outlier fraction
explain: A lower threshold demands a clearer winner, so fewer matches pass. Those that pass are less likely to be wrong, but some correct matches are lost too. Lowe's 0.8 removed 90% of false matches while losing under 5% of correct ones on the test data.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
question: A team uses 64-bit node indices plus a 16-bit tag packed into a 128-bit word and CASes it with a double-word CAS. Their threads can be descheduled for seconds. What is the honest risk statement?
options: ABA is impossible with any tag
ABA becomes very unlikely but not impossible: the 16-bit tag wraps after 65,536 successful CASes on that word
ABA is only possible on ARM
The tag makes the algorithm wait-free
explain: Michael and Scott: counters make ABA extremely unlikely but do not guarantee it never happens. At high CAS rates a 16-bit tag wraps in milliseconds, so a long stall gives many chances. With a 128-bit word there is room for a much wider tag, which is the cheap fix.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
question: Your service emits 50 GB of logs per hour and you must assign a template to every line as it arrives. Which property of a parser matters most for that?
options: It must achieve the highest possible accuracy on a labelled benchmark, whatever the cost
It must be online: constant work per line, no pass over the whole log before the first answer
It must store every raw line so templates can be recomputed later
It must know the number of distinct templates in advance to size its data structures
explain: At 33,000 to 56,000 lines per second you need bounded per-line work and no training pass. Offline parsers such as LKE are quadratic in the line count and could not finish four of five datasets in the Drain evaluation. Template counts are not knowable in advance, which is the whole problem, and retaining raw lines is a storage decision, not a parsing one.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
question: You cap Drain3 at max_clusters = 5000 with LRU eviction, and persist nothing. You restart the service. What breaks?
options: Nothing: the tree is rebuilt from the stream within a few seconds
Only the counts for templates that had been evicted before the restart
Parsing accuracy, because the LRU cache warms up in a different order
Every template id is reassigned from scratch, so every stored series, dashboard and trained model keyed on those ids silently refers to the wrong template
explain: Template ids are assigned by an incrementing counter as clusters are created. Without a persisted snapshot a restart renumbers everything in whatever order the stream happens to arrive, so id 7 now means something else. Drain3 exists partly to solve this: it snapshots state to a file, Redis or Kafka and reloads on startup. Accuracy itself recovers quickly; identity does not.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Normalisation: one event, one shape (ECS and OCSF)
question: Why keep the raw text in event.original after normalising?
options: Schemas forbid deleting fields
ECS requires it for authentication events
It makes queries faster
It lets you re-parse old events after fixing a mapping bug and shows exactly what the source said
explain: Normalised fields are an interpretation. When an interpretation turns out wrong, the original is the only way to recover the truth for past events.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The detection lifecycle: hypothesis to retirement
question: Which ADS section would have warned the team that the MFA device rule gets noisy when a popular phone launches?
options: Goal
Priority
Categorization
False Positives
explain: Known benign triggers belong in False Positives, together with how to tell them apart. FireEye's 2020 detection (lesson 16) came from exactly such an alert, investigated despite that known noise.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Tuning and allowlisting without blinding yourself
question: Which allowlist is safest for a deployment agent that triggers the PowerShell rule?
options: CommandLine contains 'DeployAgent'
Exact ParentImage path under Program Files, plus the signer and the managed-host group
ParentImage endswith `\DeployAgent.exe`
Any event from user svc_deploy
explain: Only the exact-path option uses facts an attacker cannot cheaply forge: a path standard users cannot write to, a code-signing identity, and an inventory-defined scope. The others can be met by renaming a file, adding a word, or stealing one account.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Proving it works: purple teams, emulation and metrics
question: Incident detection times this quarter were 2, 4, 6, 8 and 700 hours. Which statement is accurate?
options: The median is 6 hours; the 700-hour incident should be examined on its own
The mean, 144 hours, describes a typical incident
The median is 144 hours
Both mean and median are 6 hours
explain: Mean = 720 / 5 = 144 hours, pulled up by one case; median = 6 hours. Report both and investigate the outlier.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
question: Ring Attention with 4 ranks and contiguous chunks shows rank 3 at full utilization and rank 0 mostly idle on a causal model. Which change fixes this without changing the math?
options: Increase the block size c
Assign each rank tokens or chunks spread across the sequence (striped or zigzag)
Switch to bidirectional attention
Reduce the number of KV heads
explain: The imbalance comes from the causal triangle: later query chunks attend to more keys. Striped Attention or Llama 3's chunk i plus chunk 2CP - 1 - i assignment gives every rank the same amount of unmasked work.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
question: Saunshi et al. show the p-hop task can be solved by looping a 1-layer block floor(log2 p) + 2 times. How many loops does that give for p = 32?
explain: log2 32 = 5, plus 2 gives 7. The doubling trick is why the count grows with log2 p rather than with p: a one-hop-per-loop solution would need about 32 loops.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space
question: You must ship a small on-device model mainly for trivia-style factual QA with no retrieval. Memory is tight, latency matters. Is a looped model a good fit?
options: Yes: looping recovers the full accuracy of a 4x larger model on any task
Not really: closed-book QA depends on stored knowledge, which looping recovers poorly, and every loop adds latency
Yes: looping lowers latency because the weights stay in cache
No: looped models cannot be quantized
explain: Closed-book QA is the task group where looping closed the least of the gap (58% for k = 6) because it depends on capacity. Loops also add sequential compute. Looping shines on reasoning over context; adding retrieval (moving facts into the context) is the setting where a looped model does better.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
question: You change r from 8 to 16 but keep lora_alpha = 16. Compared with r = 8 and alpha = 16, what happens to the multiplier alpha/r?
options: It doubles from 1 to 2
It halves from 2 to 1
It stays 2, because PEFT rescales alpha automatically
It becomes alpha divided by the square root of r by default
explain: alpha/r goes from 16/8 = 2 to 16/16 = 1. With the default scaling the multiplier depends on r; only use_rslora=True switches to alpha/sqrt(r). Many recipes set alpha proportional to r (for example alpha = 2r) to keep the multiplier constant.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
question: A SISA system with S = 20 shards batches 60 uniformly random deletion requests before retraining. Roughly what fraction of the shard models must be retrained?
options: About 95%, almost every shard is hit at least once
About 5%, one shard per batch
About 33%, since 60 / 20 = 3 requests per shard on average
100% exactly, because 60 is larger than 20
explain: Each shard escapes all 60 requests with probability (1 - 1/20)^60, about 0.046, so about 95.4% of shards are hit at least once. It is not exactly 100% because some shards can get zero requests by chance. This saturation is why SISA's measured speed-ups shrink as requests pile up.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
question: A lab applies RMU to an open-weight model and publishes near-chance WMDP scores as evidence the model is safe to release. What is the strongest objection?
options: WMDP has too few questions to be meaningful
RMU always destroys general capabilities
With open weights anyone can fine-tune on related data, and RMU did not prevent relearning in the WMDP paper's own fine-tuning experiment
Near-chance scores prove the model was never trained on the data
explain: The WMDP appendix reports that fine-tuning an RMU-unlearned Mistral-7B on the forget corpus recovered performance, and Hu et al. show even benign related data can jog the knowledge back. RMU's stated threat model is a closed model unlearned just before serving, not a public release.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The PE format: headers, sections and what imports reveal
question: Where does Windows find the offset of the PE header in a file?
options: In the first two bytes, MZ
At the end of the file
In the .text section
In the 4-byte value at offset 0x3c of the MS-DOS stub
explain: Microsoft's specification: at location 0x3c the stub holds the file offset of the PE signature. In our file it was 0x80.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviours as indicators: persistence, credentials, ransomware
question: Which single event is the most urgent sign that ransomware encryption is imminent on a Windows host?
options: A new Run key value
A DNS query from a browser
A successful logon (event 4624)
vssadmin.exe deleting all shadow copies
explain: Deleting shadow copies removes a recovery option just before encryption (ATT&CK T1490). Run keys and logons happen in many benign situations; mass shadow deletion by a non-backup tool rarely does.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Sharing intelligence and writing the analysis report
question: You found an indicator in a customer's incident that could identify the customer. You want peer organisations to block it but not to learn the customer's identity. What is the best approach?
options: Post it publicly with TLP:CLEAR
Do not share anything
Share the technical indicator without identifying context, with a TLP label matching how far it may spread
Send the full report to everyone with TLP:RED
explain: Strip identifying context, keep the technical indicator, and label it (often TLP:AMBER or TLP:GREEN) so recipients know the limits. TLP:RED would stop it reaching most people who need it.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Shortlist then rerank: adaptive retrieval and funnel search
question: Single-shot exact search over 1,281,167 vectors at 2048 dims vs adaptive retrieval with D_s = 16, K = 200, D_r = 2048. Which term dominates the adaptive cost?
options: The rerank: 200 x 2048 = 409,600 multiply-adds
The shortlist scan: 16 x 1,281,167, about 20.5 million multiply-adds
Both are equal by design
Encoding the query, which grows with D_r
explain: The scan touches every vector: 20.5M multiply-adds. The rerank touches only 200 vectors: 0.41M. So the shortlist scan is about 98% of the 20.9M total, and speeding it up (smaller D_s, ANN, binary) gives the biggest win.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
question: A Llama-style 70B model is trained with 8K-token sequences on 64 GPUs (8 per node). Which configuration fits the Megatron Core guidance best?
options: TP = 4, PP = 4, CP = 2, DP = 2
TP = 64, nothing else
TP = 1, PP = 64
TP = 16 across two nodes, DP = 4
explain: This is the guide's own example: TP stays inside a node, PP splits the 80 layers across nodes, CP = 2 handles the 8K sequence, and DP uses what is left (4 x 4 x 2 x 2 = 64). TP = 64 or 16 crosses nodes with all-reduces every layer; PP = 64 gives a huge bubble.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: An image is not a photograph: smear, footprint and checks
question: An analyst finds that one process's "next" pointer leads to bytes that are not a valid process object. What is the most cautious reading?
options: It proves a rootkit unlinked the process
The image must be discarded
It may be smear from a process that exited during acquisition; confirm with an independent method before calling it tampering
The acquisition tool wrote fake data
explain: Pages are copied at different moments, so a stale pointer is a normal smear effect. Unlinking by malware is possible too, which is exactly why you compare the list walk with a scan.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: VADs and malfind: finding code that has no file
question: malfind reports a 1 MB private PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE region in notepad.exe whose first bytes are MZ. Which is the best next step?
options: Ignore it; malfind always has false positives
Dump the region, scan it with YARA and parse it as a PE, and check for threads starting inside it
Delete notepad.exe from the disk image
Re-acquire memory until the region disappears
explain: A large executable private region starting with a PE header inside a simple program is a strong lead. Extract it and analyse it; threads starting there would confirm it runs.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Cobalt Strike Beacon in memory: finding and reading its configuration
question: You find the bytes 2e 2f 2e 2f 2e 2c at the start of a block in a rundll32.exe region. What is the most likely reading?
options: A Cobalt Strike version 4 Beacon configuration: XOR 0x2E gives setting 1, type 1, length 2
A PE header
A Linux ELF file
Random data; config blocks have no fixed start
explain: Decoded with 0x2E the bytes are 00 01 00 01 00 02: setting 1 (BeaconType), type short, length 2. That fixed start is what parsers search for.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Case: Ivanti Connect Secure, and a memory-first workflow
question: In the Ivanti case, why could Volexity not rely on the appliance's logs to confirm exploitation?
options: The appliance had no logging feature
Logs were encrypted by Ivanti
The exploit requests did not appear in the logs even with unauthenticated request logging, and the attacker cleared or disabled logging in at least one case
Volexity had no access to the appliance
explain: Volexity reports both points. The memory sample, by contrast, held evidence of the exploit chain itself.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Why freed memory does not go back: pages, arenas, purging
question: In the 64-objects-per-page model, a workload frees 95% of its objects at random. What fraction of pages becomes returnable?
options: About 95%
About 3.8%
About 50%
Exactly 0%
explain: A page is empty only if all 64 objects died: 0.95^64 is about 0.0375, so about 3.8% of pages. The other 96% each hold at least one survivor and stay resident. Correlated lifetimes in real programs do better than this random model.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
question: A spin lock is implemented as `while LOCKED.swap(true, Acquire) {}` ... critical section ... `LOCKED.store(false, ORD)`. Which ORD is the weakest correct choice?
options: Relaxed
Acquire
SeqCst, because unlocking must be globally visible
Release
explain: The unlock must publish the critical section's writes to the next locker. That needs a Release store paired with the Acquire swap. Acquire is not even allowed on a plain store, Relaxed creates no happens-before, and SeqCst works but promises far more than needed.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
question: A developer removes the re-validation step: after `hp[me] = t; full_fence();` the code reads `t->next` directly. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, the fence already makes the hazard pointer visible
Another thread may have retired and freed t before the hazard pointer was published, so reading its next field touches freed memory
The CAS will always fail
The retired list will grow without bound
explain: Publishing only protects a node that is still in the structure at the moment the slot becomes visible. If t was unlinked and a scan ran between the load and the publish, the scan saw no slot and freed t. The re-read proves t was still reachable after the publish, so every later scan must see the slot.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
question: A Rust program uses crossbeam-epoch. Memory grows steadily, and a profiler shows one thread blocked on a channel receive inside a function that holds an `epoch::Guard`. What fixes it?
options: Increase the bag size from 64
Drop the guard (or call repin) before blocking on the channel
Switch the CAS to SeqCst (sequentially consistent) ordering
Call `pin()` more often on other threads
explain: The blocked thread stays pinned in an old epoch, so the global epoch cannot advance past it and every thread's garbage waits. Bag size and memory ordering do not change that. Holding guards only for short, non-blocking sections is the rule for any grace-period scheme.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Heap overflow: corrupting the neighbouring object
question: On Linux with glibc, a heap overflow often crashes later inside free() rather than at the bad write. What explains that?
options: free() is unsafe
The kernel delays signals
The overflow corrupted the allocator's size header of the next block, and free() trusts that header
glibc does not use headers
explain: glibc keeps a size header before each block. Overwriting it does not fault immediately; the allocator only notices, or misbehaves, when it later reads that corrupted size.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Uninitialized memory and type confusion
question: Why did build_reply print hunter2 although it never touched check_password's variable?
options: printf prints its previous output again when a buffer is empty
The compiler merged the two arrays on purpose
check_password returned the secret in a register that printf read
Both functions' frames used the same stack addresses, and returning from check_password left its bytes in place
explain: Frames are reused, not wiped. The uninitialized reply started with the bytes check_password left behind.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
question: A model trained on the Market-1501 training identities reaches high accuracy on held-out images of those same people. Why does that not tell you it will work for re-ID on Market-1501's test split?
options: Because the test images are smaller than training images
Because accuracy is not defined for embeddings
Because the test identities are different people, so what matters is whether distances generalize to unseen identities
Because re-ID only uses the gallery, never the query
explain: Re-ID test identities are disjoint from training identities. Closed-set accuracy on known people says little about whether the embedding separates new people. You need a retrieval evaluation on unseen identities.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
question: Your team wants to add k-reciprocal re-ranking to a live system that searches a gallery growing by millions of crops per day. What is the main concern?
options: It needs labeled data to retrain the model
It needs neighbor lists for gallery images too, so its cost grows with the gallery and must be recomputed as it changes
It only improves rank-1, never mAP
It only works with ArcFace features
explain: Re-ranking is unsupervised and needs no retraining, but it computes reciprocal neighbors from the gallery's own top-k lists. That is affordable on a fixed benchmark gallery and costly on a large, changing one.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
question: In a JMH run with forks set to 0, benchmark C is 30% slower when it runs after benchmark D than when it runs alone. What is the right fix?
options: Run each benchmark in its own forked JVM, as JMH does by default
Increase warm-up iterations so the JIT settles
Disable ASLR
Add a Blackhole to benchmark C
explain: C inherits JIT profiles from D in a shared JVM, the effect JMHSample_12_Forking demonstrates. More warm-up in the same JVM keeps the polluted profile. ASLR and Blackholes address layout noise and dead code, which are not the problem here.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
question: You serve a MoE with NVFP4 on B200s to speed up rollout but keep the trainer in BF16 to save engineering time. What do the Miles docs say?
options: Supported; add R3 to cover the drift
Supported only with --use-tis
Supported only on Hopper
Unsupported: NVFP4 rollout needs an NVFP4 trainer forward
explain: The compatibility table allows BF16 training with BF16, FP8 block-wise or MXFP8 rollout, but NVFP4 rollout pairs only with NVFP4 training. The report explains that NVFP4 requires every stage that touches the weights to quantize them.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
question: LRB samples training examples uniformly over objects in the memory window rather than over requests. Why?
options: Sampling requests would be too slow to compute
Sampling requests over-represents popular objects, while the decisions LRB must learn are mostly about rarely requested objects it should evict
GBMs cannot train on duplicate objects
Objects that are never requested again would be sampled too often
explain: Per-request sampling picks a hot object once per request, so the dataset fills with objects that should obviously stay. The good evictions, objects beyond the boundary including those never requested again, would be rare. The paper samples over objects so both kinds are represented.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Inside an APK and an IPA: what anyone can download and read
question: A client ships an update and its users report that it will not install over the old version: 'App not installed'. The release engineer used a new signing key. Why does Android refuse?
options: The new key's certificate has expired
Android compares the update's certificate with the installed app's and allows the update only if they match (or the new key was rotated in with proof from the old one)
The new APK is missing classes.dex
Google Play must countersign every certificate
explain: The package name plus the signing key are the app's identity, so an unrelated new key looks like a different author. Android's docs say a new certificate means a new package name and a separate app. The certificate in our output is self-signed and valid until 2043, so expiry and CA countersigning are not the issue.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Android IPC: exported components, intent redirection, PendingIntents
question: Your app forwards an intent from an extra, but only after checking `next.component?.packageName == packageName`. Is that enough?
options: Yes: if the target is inside our own app, nothing can go wrong

No: forwarding to the app's own non-exported components is exactly the danger, and grant flags or extras can still be attacker-chosen; allowlist the specific component and extras and strip grant flags
Yes, as long as the activity is exported
No, because package names can be spoofed by the sender
explain: Intent redirection is dangerous precisely because the target is inside your app: the attacker borrows your identity to reach your private components and providers. Checking 'it is our package' lets all of that through. Android's guidance is to check the exact destination and clear the URI-grant flags, as IntentSanitizer does.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Local authentication: a fingerprint must unlock a key, not a boolean
question: A password manager wants the vault to stop opening if a new fingerprint is added to the phone. Which iOS access control flag fits?
options: .userPresence
.biometryCurrentSet
.devicePasscode
kSecAttrAccessibleAlways
explain: Apple's documentation: with .biometryCurrentSet the item is invalidated if fingers are added or removed, or Face ID is re-enrolled. .userPresence stays usable after enrollment changes and also accepts the passcode. The last option is not an access control flag for biometrics at all.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
question: Why didn't DeepSeek simply use MQA, which has an even smaller cache than MLA?
options: MQA cannot be used with a KV cache
In their 7B ablation MQA lost clearly to MHA on hard benchmarks, and they wanted MHA-level quality
MQA needs more GPU memory for weights
MQA does not support causal masking
explain: DeepSeek-V2 Appendix D.1 shows MQA at 37.9 MMLU vs 45.2 for MHA at 7B. MLA was designed to get a small cache without paying that quality cost.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Build an MLA layer and prove the two forms agree
question: A decoder caches the latent before RMSNorm and applies the norm when reading it back. The plain form normalizes before up-projecting. Do the two still agree?
options: Yes: RMSNorm acts on each token's latent alone, so normalizing at write time or at read time gives the same vectors; it only costs repeated work on every read
No: RMSNorm mixes information across tokens
No: the norm must come after absorption
Yes, but only if the RoPE key is normalized too
explain: RMSNorm is per token, so both orders give identical vectors; DeepSeek's code normalizes once on write because every later step reads it. What does break the match is normalizing the 64-wide RoPE key (the plain form never does) or skipping the norm on one side.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Why serving one model per fine-tune wastes GPUs
question: 100 merged 7B fine-tunes would fit on a large cluster. Why is serving them as separate models still inefficient when each gets little traffic?
options: Merged models are slower per token than the base model
Each model decodes tiny batches, so most of each weight read serves only one or two tokens
Merged weights cannot use the KV cache
The adapters must be recomputed for every token
explain: Decode is bandwidth bound: the cost of a step is dominated by reading the weights, and batching shares that read. Splitting traffic across 100 copies leaves each with batch sizes near 1, so GPU time per token stays high.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Multi-LoRA in vLLM and LoRAX, and the cost model
question: You serve adapters of rank 8 and 16 with vLLM but set --max-lora-rank 256. What is the main consequence?
options: Requests fail because ranks must match exactly
Adapters are automatically retrained at rank 256
Throughput improves because larger slots are faster
GPU memory is reserved for rank-256 slots, wasting space that the KV cache could use
explain: vLLM preallocates each of the max_loras slots at max_lora_rank and pads smaller adapters into them. The docs warn that setting it much higher than needed wastes memory and can hurt performance.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: How N trades recall against latency and cost
question: Searches run in parallel and the LLM rewrite takes 600 ms. You raise N from 4 to 8. Which effect is largest, under the model in this lesson?
options: End-to-end latency roughly doubles
Latency and load both stay the same
Recall doubles
End-to-end latency rises a little, while retriever load and candidate count roughly double
explain: In parallel, the search phase grows with the slowest of N (about m H_N: 83 ms to 109 ms at m = 40), small next to 600 ms of LLM time. But every extra query is another search to serve and more candidates downstream, so load and context grow linearly. Recall gains shrink as N grows.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Bi-encoder, late interaction, cross-encoder: where the cost goes
question: Which scorer could you put directly over a 50-million-document index as the **first** stage?
options: A cross-encoder, if you batch on a large GPU
A bi-encoder or late-interaction model, because document vectors are precomputed and searchable with ANN
Only BM25; neural models cannot be first stages
duoBERT with the SAMPLE aggregation
explain: First stages need precomputed document representations so the query can be matched with an index. Bi-encoders give one vector per document; ColBERT indexes token vectors and retrieves end to end. A cross-encoder has nothing to index: it needs a forward pass per pair.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
question: During training, what does the head that predicts x(t+3) receive as input at position t?
options: The shared representation of the prefix x(1..t) only
The prefix plus head 1's and head 2's predicted tokens
The true tokens x(t+1) and x(t+2), via teacher forcing
The whole sequence, with future tokens masked out after the loss
